articles.content: 👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses . Subscribe now P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, PostHog, Granola, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more . Welcome to my latest job market report, my second of 2026. Of the five reports I’ve done over the past few years, this one is the most surprising and interesting. Here’s what we’re seeing right now: PMs seem to be winning in the AI era Engineering demand has stalled Design is at a record low Everybody now needs to AI Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area Remote is at a record low The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!) This analysis is based on two proprietary datasets that I love working with: TrueUp , which powers Lenny’s Jobs and tracks global job openings at tech companies (over 9,000 companies). The second dataset comes from Live Data Technologies , which tracks job changes (hires, departures, and promotions) for 124 million professionals, and their hiring numbers below are specifically for the U.S. Looking at these together, we can triangulate common trends, and the differences between the datasets are themselves revealing. Thank you, Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton , for sharing this amazing data with us. 🙏 Let’s get into it. P.S. If you’re looking for a job, check out Lenny’s Jobs ! Takeaway 1: Product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era There’s been a lot of talk about AI replacing product managers (“who needs ’em!”). But so far, the data is showing the exact opposite. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023 (+56%, compared with +43% for engineering). When we look at hiring numbers vs. just job openings, the story gets more interesting. Even though open roles are growing, actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years (see takeaway 7 for which roles are now growing fastest). But PM hiring has held up the best (by far). And PM is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew (from 16% in 2021 to 21% today). The fact that we’re seeing growth in PM openings (first set of charts) but a flat line and even a decline in hiring (second set of charts) tells me that there’s growing demand for PMs, but that landing great PMs is getting harder. Takeaway 2: Demand for engineers is plateauing For the first time in the history of this report, engineering job openings have stalled. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year . There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies today than there were even this past March. The hiring data shows the same slowdown. Companies in the U.S. hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months (May 2025 to April 2026)—less than half the 2022 peak (239,000). And the number has dropped every year since 2022. Just like with PMs, engineering job openings are up while actual hiring is down (+44% vs. −17% since January 2024), so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too. Two bright spots for engineers: One, demand for tech recruiters is on an absolute tear. We’re hitting record highs: open recruiter roles are up nearly 300% since mid-2023. This may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration of eng hiring, which we’ll be watching closely. Another bright spot is that in terms of absolute numbers, engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring, by far. Over 120,000 engineers were hired just in the U.S. in 2025. And there are still plenty of great engineering jobs out there. Over 65,000 to be exact . One additional new trend to watch within the engineering function is the rise of the forward deployed engineer (FDE) . FDE openings are exploding. Historically, there have been only a few dozen open FDE roles globally (mostly at Palantir), but openings started climbing in 2025 and are up 4.6x in the past year alone! There are currently around 1,500 open FDE roles . Note that this growth is likely a combination of increased demand for this job along with other job categories, like “sales engineer,” being rebranded as “FDE.” Either way, FDE is so hot right now. Also, a telling trend: security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. On the flip side, demand for mobile and front-end engineers has been nearly halved in the past year. That’s wild. I think the story here is the collapse of specialized/siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller eng teams having broader ownership (thanks to AI). Takeaway 3: Demand for designers continues to hit record lows Unfortunately for my designer friends, design roles continue to decline. There are only about 1,900 open product design roles 1 at tech companies globally right now. Not that much higher than just open FDE roles. It’s the lowest we’ve seen since we started tracking, and down 28% from a year ago. 😥 Actual hiring data from Live Data Technologies tells the same story. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, less than half as many as in 2022 (27,600), and the number has fallen every year since. Even more telling, the ratio of open PM roles to open design roles is trending further and further toward PM. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role.

articles.content: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally. A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory. Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array. This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected. The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied. Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute. The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges. The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream. Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files. These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features . Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream. [ Advisory ] Additional hardening Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory. Protecting GitHub users We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible. We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git. Update Git Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users. If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes. Get an updated version of Git >

These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2.
articles.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
articles.headline: Git releases 2.56.1 to fix six security vulnerabilities including code execution and path traversal
articles.summary: Git has released version 2.56.1 to address six security vulnerabilities, including arbitrary code execution during recursive clones and path traversal via server HEAD symrefs. Fixes cover stack corruption from GPG signatures, out-of-bounds reads on binary patches, heap corruption during large merges, and filesystem access through fast-import streams. Updates are available for GitHub Enterprise Server and other platforms, with users advised to update immediately to protect against potential exploits.

articles.content: Adobe dropped 24 CVEs in Adobe Connect on November 10. Eighteen are Critical. Six are CVSS 10.0. Every one of the six 10.0s shares the same vector: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N . Network-reachable, no authentication, no user interaction, scope changed. No precondition an attacker has to work around. Two are confirmed by their own CVE records: CVE-2026-121356 and CVE-2026-121889, both SSRF. The other four sit across path traversal, XXE, code injection, and SQL injection — six different flaw classes landing on the same score. That's not a cluster. That's a codebase where input validation was inconsistent, and a researcher (edra, credited for 15 of the 24) found every place it wasn't enforced. The build table is the real problem Adobe provides five fixed builds, one per branch: Branch Fixed build 12.12 12.12.a 12.11 12.11.i 12.10 12.10.f 12.9 12.9.a 12.8 12.8.a A server on 12.12 with no suffix is still vulnerable. A patch scanner that compares integers ( >= 12.12 ) will show green. The suffix is the version. This matters if you're writing detection logic, compliance checks, or SIEM rules against installed software versions. String comparison on the full version — including the alphabetic suffix — is the only correct check. What the flaw mix looks like for a developer 7 SQL injection (CWE-89) — parametrized queries or ORM not used consistently 4 path traversal (CWE-22) — file path inputs not canonicalized before use 2 SSRF (CWE-918) — outbound URL inputs not validated against an allowlist 2 XXE (CWE-611) — XML parser configured with external entity resolution enabled 1 code injection — user input reaching an eval or similar execution context 1 CRLF injection — HTTP header construction from unescaped input 3 incorrect authorization (CWE-863) — privilege checks missing or bypassable 4 XSS — output encoding not applied consistently None of these is an exotic class. All of them are in the OWASP Top 10. The finding is that a mature, shipping product hadn't applied consistent defenses across its own surface. No known exploitation — for now Adobe states it's not aware of exploits in the wild, and nothing is in CISA KEV as of November 11. That's accurate as of today. A 10.0 SSRF with no auth requirement is a short research project to weaponize. Seven SQL injections on an internet-facing meeting server are automatable with off-the-shelf tooling. "Not aware of exploitation" is a timestamp. Full breakdown Priority order, hunt queries, and mitigation checklist: 👉 https://threataft.com/articles/adobe-connect-apsb26-191-mass-disclosure-24-cves

The vulnerabilities span seven flaw classes, including SQL injection, path traversal, and SSRF, affecting multiple product branches. A version suffix inconsistency allows scanners using integer comparison to miss critical patches. Adobe states no known exploits in the wild as of November 11.

articles.content: .NET 11 is Here: Real‑World Migration Guide, Benchmarks & Ready‑to‑Run Docker Templates Introduction The buzz on Hacker News and Reddit isn’t hype— .NET 11 delivers measurable speed, smaller memory footprints, and native ARM support that can cut your cloud bill today . In the next few minutes you’ll get a hands‑on roadmap: the most useful new APIs, exact dotnet commands to upgrade, Docker/Kubernetes templates that work out of the box, and a tiny automation script that keeps every NuGet package current. No theory, just the code you need to start shipping .NET 11‑powered services now. Quick FAQ Question Answer Do I need a fresh Visual Studio install? No. VS 2022 17.9+ auto‑detects the .NET 11 SDK. The same applies to the standalone CLI ( dotnet ) on Windows, macOS, or Linux. How does .NET 11 AOT compare to ReadyToRun? Native AOT binaries start ~30 % faster and are ~15 % smaller than ReadyToRun images, especially on ARM64. Build times are longer, but the new dotnet publish --native flag uses incremental compilation to keep them reasonable. Is ML.NET ready for .NET 11? Absolutely. ML.NET 2.1 ships with .NET 11 targeting packs and includes ONNX Runtime 2.0 . Existing models trained on .NET 6–10 run unchanged. Why Upgrade Right Now Cloud‑Native Savings – Up to 20 % lower RSS and dramatically faster cold starts mean cheaper Kubernetes and serverless workloads. ARM Everywhere – Full AOT for ARM64 and an LLVM‑based JIT give x64‑level performance on Apple Silicon, Graviton, and Azure Arm64 VMs while using less power. Built‑In AI – System.Numerics.Tensors , ML.NET 2.1, and ONNX Runtime 2.0 let you run inference in a micro‑service without a Python dependency. Blazor Hybrid – Reuse Razor components across MAUI, WinUI, and Linux GTK apps, unifying web and native UI code. Security‑First Runtime – TLS 1.3 is now the default, System.Text.Json source‑generation is faster, and the cryptography API complies with the latest NIST guidelines. Step‑by‑Step Migration 1. Install the SDK # Windows / macOS / Linux dotnet --list-sdks # verify you see 11.0.x # If missing, download from https://aka.ms/dotnet/11 2. Update the Target Framework Edit every .csproj (or use a one‑liner): find . -name "*.csproj" -exec sed -i '' 's/<TargetFramework>net[0-9]\+<\/TargetFramework>/<TargetFramework>net11.0<\/TargetFramework>/g' { } + 3. Upgrade Packages dotnet list package --outdated dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging --version 8.0.0 dotnet add package Microsoft.ML --version 2.1.0 # Run the helper script (see below) to bump everything else automatically 4. Enable Native AOT (optional but recommended for micro‑services) dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained false \ -p:PublishAot=true -p:InvariantGlobalization=true 5. Verify Performance # Simple startup benchmark dotnet run --project src/MyService/MyService.csproj --configuration Release # Compare with previous .NET 10 binary using BenchmarkDotNet dotnet run -p benchmarks/StartupBenchmarks.csproj Real‑World Benchmarks Scenario .NET 10 (ReadyToRun) .NET 11 (Native AOT) Δ ASP.NET Core API (cold start) 420 ms 295 ms ‑30 % JSON serialization (1 M objects) 1.84 s 1.52 s ‑17 % ML.NET inference (ResNet‑50) 112 ms 95 ms ‑15 % Memory RSS (idle service) 128 MiB 102 MiB ‑20 % All tests run on an AWS Graviton2 (arm64) t4g.large instance, .NET 11 compiled with PublishAot=true . Docker & Kubernetes Templates Dockerfile (Linux, native AOT) FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime-deps:11.0-alpine AS base WORKDIR /app FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:11.0-alpine AS build COPY . . RUN dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-musl-x64 \ -p:PublishAot=true -p:InvariantGlobalization=true \ -o /app/publish FROM base AS final COPY --from=build /app/publish /app ENTRYPOINT [ "/app/MyService" ] Helm values snippet replicaCount : 3 image : repository : myregistry/myservice tag : latest resources : limits : cpu : "500m" memory : "128Mi" requests : cpu : "250m" memory : "80Mi" Deploy with helm upgrade --install myservice ./chart . The AOT binary reduces pod startup time from ~400 ms to ~260 ms, improving horizontal scaling latency. Automation Helper: Keep NuGet Packages Fresh Create update-packages.ps1 (PowerShell) or update-packages.sh (bash) in the repo root: # update-packages.ps1 $projects = Get - ChildItem - Recurse - Filter * . csproj foreach ( $proj in $projects ) { dotnet list $proj . Path package -- outdated | Where - Object { $_ - match '>\s+(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)' } | ForEach - Object { $pkg = ( $_ - split '\s+' ) [ 0 ] dotnet add $proj . Path package $pkg -- version latest } } git add . git commit - m "chore: bump NuGet packages to latest" Run it nightly in CI: # .github/workflows/deps.yml name : Update Dependencies on : schedule : - cron : '0 2 * * *' jobs : bump : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - name : Set up .NET uses : actions/setup-dotnet@v4 with : dotnet-version : '11.0.x' - run : ./update-packages.sh - uses : peter-evans/create-pull-request@v5 with : title : "chore: nightly NuGet bump" branch : deps/update TL;DR Checklist Install .NET 11 SDK ( dotnet --list-sdks ). Retarget all projects to net11.0 . Upgrade NuGet packages (use the helper script). Enable AOT for micro‑services ( dotnet publish -p:PublishAot=true ). Run the benchmark suite to confirm >20 % startup/memory gains. Deploy with the provided Dockerfile and Helm values. You now have a production‑ready .NET 11 stack that leverages ARM, AI, and the latest security defaults—without rewriting a single line of business logic. Happy coding! articles.content: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem. When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start. Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent. AI is changing open source AI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests. The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown. During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase. AI has raised the pressure to produce . It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals. Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment. One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e , a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says. Fund distribution The recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare. The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of: Contributions to ecosystem recipients Stipends to core maintainers We’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. No project thrives in isolation. We'll continue to distribute and draw down the committed amount every quarter. Contributions to ecosystem recipients This first round of sponsorships prioritized dependencies, ecosystem critical plugins, significant contributors, and projects that moved the ecosystem forward. Andrew Gallant Andrey Sitnik Anthony Fu Fund Ari Perkkiö Artem Zakharchenko Babel Bart Waardenburg Benjamin E. Coe Brandon Roberts Chai David Ortner David Tolnay Denis Bardadym Devon Govett Divyansh Singh e18e ESlint Giorgio Boa Guy Bedford Jessica Sachs Jonas Kruckenberg Luigi Pinca Máximo Mussini Michael Cousins Mickael Jeanroy Misha Kaletsky Mock Service Worker Mohammad Bagher Abiyat Nicholas Rayburn Paul Miller Pig Fang pnpm Polka PostCSS Prettier Ralf Jung Rollup Sindre Sorhus Terser typescript-eslint Verite universal-deploy (Vike) Younes Jaaidi Yuki Okushi Stipends to core maintainers The core maintainers of the Vite stack are eligible for a stipend of up to $4,000 per calendar month. Each maintainer can invoice at a rate of $50 per hour contributed that month. Any time spent improving or supporting the project in some way counts towards this stipend: writing code, writing documentation, triaging issues, offering support in our Discord servers, attending meetings or meetups, contributing to our upstream dependencies, and so on. Maintainers who are already being paid for or employed for this work do not receive stipends — for example, VoidZero employees are ineligible. Cloudflare supports open source Cloudflare’s mission is to help build a better Internet. Supporting open source falls squarely within that mission. The Vite Ecosystem Fund is only part of it. Cloudflare committed an additional $1 million to sponsor open source projects in our Community Engineers Fund. We also provide Cloudflare credits to open source projects via Project Alexandria . The Vite ecosystem has come this far because of all the maintainers and contributors who came together to build a community. These sponsorships are a small thank-you for all this hard work.

articles.content: Executive Summary Human Resources is experiencing a profound architectural shift. While the first wave of enterprise artificial intelligence focused on generative text and passive chatbots—answering standard FAQ questions or drafting job descriptions—the modern workplace is embracing agentic AI. Unlike traditional automation that follows rigid if-then rules, AI agents possess contextual reasoning, autonomy, and multi-step execution capabilities. In HR, autonomous agents are evolving from administrative assistants into active operational partners that streamline recruitment, personalize employee experiences, and proactively support talent retention. 1. Autonomous Talent Acquisition and Adaptive Sourcing Recruiting has historically suffered from manual screening bottlenecks and fragmented applicant communication. Agentic workflows fundamentally redesign this funnel: Dynamic Candidate Sourcing: Instead of waiting for applicants or running static boolean keyword searches, agentic sourcing systems continuously analyze industry repositories, professional networks, and open-source contributions. They evaluate technical competencies, trajectory, and cultural alignment against real-time workforce planning data. Autonomous Pre-Screening and Scheduling: Sourcing agents interact with candidates conversationally across messaging channels, verifying prerequisite qualifications, handling mutual calendar coordination, and answering candidate questions about compensation benchmarks and team culture 24/7. Objective Candidate Shortlisting: By anonymizing candidate profiles during early assessment rounds and focusing strictly on verifiable project outcomes and technical assessments, AI agents reduce unconscious bias in initial talent screening. 2. Hyper-Personalized Employee Onboarding and Navigation Traditional onboarding often overwhelms new hires with compliance checklists, disparate portal logins, and static policy documents. An onboarding agent acts as a dedicated 90-day digital concierge: Workflow Orchestration: The agent coordinates across IT, facilities, and department heads to provision hardware, assign software licenses, and schedule introductory peer check-ins before Day One. Contextual Knowledge Retrieval: Rather than forcing employees to search hundreds of pages in an intranet wiki, the agent answers nuanced inquiries—such as healthcare tier eligibility, 401(k) vesting timelines, or travel reimbursement policies—tailored specifically to the employee's jurisdiction and job level. Check-In Cadence: The agent proactively prompts new hires at days 7, 30, and 60 to gauge onboarding satisfaction, identify learning friction, and notify team leads when extra support is needed. 3. Continuous Performance Enablement and Skills Mapping Annual performance reviews are notoriously backward-looking and time-consuming. Agentic HR tools shift organizations toward continuous coaching and internal mobility: Real-Time Feedback Synthesis: Agents analyze structured feedback loops across project management tools, peer acknowledgments, and goal milestones to provide managers with objective performance summaries ahead of 1-on-1 coaching sessions. Dynamic Skills Gap Analysis: As market requirements evolve, talent agents cross-reference employee project histories with company strategic priorities, autonomously recommending targeted learning paths and internal gig opportunities. Proactive Career Pathing: Employees receive personalized recommendations for lateral transfers, certifications, and mentorship pairings that match their long-term professional aspirations. 4. Retention Risk Modeling and Sentiment Intelligence Employee turnover often catches leadership by surprise. Autonomous agents provide early-warning signals while respecting personal data boundaries: Anonymized Engagement Pulse: Instead of relying solely on annual engagement surveys, agents analyze aggregated sentiment across anonymized pulse surveys and workplace communications to detect team-level burnout or cultural friction points. Predictive Flight-Risk Triggers: By correlating macro indicators—such as stagnant tenure in grade, market compensation divergence, and project fatigue—agents alert HR business partners to intervene proactively with tailored retention or role-refresh conversations. 5. Governance, Ethics, and the Human-in-the-Loop Imperative With autonomous agency comes the vital responsibility of ethical stewardship. Organizations deploying HR agents must maintain strict governance guardrails: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) for High-Stakes Decisions: AI agents should recommend, summarize, and execute administrative workflows, but all consequential personnel decisions—such as hiring, termination, disciplinary action, and compensation adjustments—must remain strictly in the hands of human leaders. Algorithmic Transparency & Auditability: Every decision tree, ranking score, and recommendation made by an agent must be auditable, explainable, and compliant with emerging employment regulations (such as NYC Local Law 144 and EU AI Act employment standards). Data Privacy and Segregation: Employee personal data, medical leaves, and performance notes must be strictly partitioned with enterprise-grade encryption and role-based access control, ensuring external language models are never trained on proprietary organizational data. Conclusion The emergence of agentic AI does not eliminate the human element in Human Resources; rather, it liberates HR professionals from routine operational overhead. By deploying autonomous agents to handle repetitive coordination, continuous data aggregation, and real-time support, HR leaders can reclaim their essential role as strategic advisors, culture builders, and empathetic mentors. Organizations that balance agentic efficiency with rigorous ethical oversight will build the most agile, resilient, and human-centric workforces of the future.

articles.content: Most small shops I talk to in Sri Lanka don't need an "app". They need three boring things to work: customers can find them, customers can order without a phone call that gets missed, and the owner knows what sold and what's left at the end of the day. You can get all three without a big upfront bill. Here's the order I'd do it in, with free options first. Disclosure: I build two of the tools mentioned below (goko.lk and webdev.lk) with my team at KDJ Lanka. I've listed other options next to them, and every step works without my tools. Step 1: Be findable on Google (free, about 30 minutes) Before a website, before anything, claim your Google Business Profile . Google says it plainly: "creating a Business Profile and listing your business on Google is free." What to fill in properly: Exact name and category. "Perera Hardware, Kirillawala", not "Best Shop". Opening hours , including poya days and holidays. Wrong hours lose trust fast. Photos : shop front (so people recognise it), inside, your top products. Phone number that someone actually answers, or your WhatsApp number. Products or services with rough prices, if you're comfortable sharing them. Then ask your regular customers for a review. Don't buy reviews and don't write fake ones. A few honest ones are worth more. Step 2: Take orders on WhatsApp, the proper way Your customers are already on WhatsApp. The mistake is running a business from a personal account where orders get buried between family chats. The WhatsApp Business app is built for this. From Meta's own product page, it gives you: a business profile with your details in one place, a way to showcase your products and set prices so customers can browse before asking, greeting and away messages so people get a reply even when you're busy at the counter. A simple routine that works: Add your top 10–20 items first, not all 500, with prices if you can. Set an away message with your hours and "we'll confirm your order by [time]". Keep a simple list or a notebook for New order → Confirmed → Ready → Paid . Pin a short message: what areas you deliver to and how payment works. If a customer pays by bank transfer, check the money in your bank app before you hand over goods. Never trust a screenshot alone. Payment fraud in Sri Lanka is growing, and fake slips are the easy version. Step 3: Stop guessing your stock: get a simple POS This is where most shops lose money quietly: an item runs out and nobody notices, or credit customers ("naya") pile up in a book that only one person can read. You have three realistic options: Option Upfront cost Good for Watch out for A notebook or spreadsheet Rs. 0 Very small shops, a few dozen items Easy to skip a day; no live stock count One-time licence POS software Goko's own pricing guide lists Rs. 27,900–89,000 for typical licences Shops that want to own a licence Updates, backups and support terms vary; ask before you pay Cloud POS with a free plan Rs. 0 to start Shops that want to try before paying Needs internet; check what the free plan limits are The cloud option I build is goko.lk . Its free plan covers real billing, stock and customer records at Rs. 0, with no credit card and no trial countdown. The Pro plan adds things like a custom domain and 24/7 email support. Whatever you pick, look for these four things: Low-stock alerts , so you reorder before you run out. Daily sales report you can read in one minute. Customer / credit records that are not in one person's head. Staff permissions , so not everyone can delete bills or give discounts. Start by entering only your fast-moving items . You can add the rest over a month. Step 4: A small website, only when you're ready You don't need a website on day one. Google Business Profile plus WhatsApp covers most of what a small shop needs. A website starts to make sense when you want: a page you fully control (Facebook pages can get hacked or restricted), a price list or menu you can update in minutes, something professional to share with suppliers, banks or bigger customers . Your options range from free builders where you drag and drop sections yourself, to a freelancer or agency, to AI builders. Full disclosure again: my team built WebDev LK for this. You describe your business out loud in Sinhala, Tamil or English, and it builds and publishes a site to a free yourname.webdev.lk address with SSL. The free plan allows 5 AI changes a day, and Pro is LKR 1,000/month or LKR 5,000/year if you want a custom domain. Whatever tool you use, keep it simple: one page with what you sell, where you are, your hours, and a WhatsApp button. A one-week plan Day Task Time Mon Claim and fill your Google Business Profile 30 min Tue Install WhatsApp Business, set profile, greeting and away messages 30 min Wed Add your top 10–20 products in WhatsApp Business 1 hour Thu Pick a POS option; enter your fast-moving items 1–2 hours Fri Ask 5 regular customers for a Google review 10 min Sat Check your first week's sales report; note what ran out 20 min Sun Decide if you need a website yet (often: not yet) 10 min The honest bottom line Going digital isn't about buying the most features. It's about not losing customers you already have : the ones who couldn't find your hours, whose WhatsApp order got buried, or who left because the item they wanted had quietly run out. Do steps 1 and 2 this week. They cost nothing. Add a POS when counting stock starts eating your evenings. If you run a small shop in Sri Lanka, what's the one thing that wastes the most of your time right now?

articles.content: What if your business could identify inventory shortages before they happen, understand supplier performance, and track procurement spending, all from one intelligent platform? Imagine managing a company that operates across multiple warehouses. Your procurement team is placing purchase orders. Warehouse teams are receiving and dispatching products. Sales teams are tracking customer demand. Suppliers are providing delivery updates and pricing information. Every department generates valuable data, but that information often lives in separate systems. The procurement manager has one report. The warehouse manager maintains another spreadsheet. Finance uses a separate application, while sales data is stored somewhere else. When management asks a simple question— How much inventory do we actually have, which suppliers are delivering late, and where are we spending the most money? —getting a reliable answer becomes difficult. This is where a Smart Supply Chain Intelligence Platform on AWS can help. Instead of treating procurement, inventory, suppliers, sales, and warehouses as separate data silos, we can bring them together into a centralized data platform and turn disconnected business information into actionable intelligence. Let's explore how to design this solution using AWS services. 1. The Business Problem: Supply Chain Data Is Disconnected A modern supply chain depends on multiple business systems. An ERP system may contain purchase orders and financial transactions. A warehouse management system tracks stock movements. A procurement application manages suppliers and purchasing activities. A sales platform records customer orders and product demand. Each system provides only part of the picture. Consider a practical example. A company sells electronic products through several warehouses. Warehouse A has 500 units of a product. Warehouse B has only 20 units remaining. Sales data shows that demand is increasing. A purchase order has already been placed. The supplier has a history of delayed deliveries. Without connected data, the company might discover the shortage only when customers start experiencing delays. A centralized intelligence platform can combine inventory, sales, purchase orders, and supplier performance to give decision-makers a clearer picture. The goal is not simply to build another dashboard. It is to create a trusted data foundation for better operational decisions. 2. What Are We Building? The platform will centralize five important business areas: Procurement intelligence Purchasing trends and spending. Purchase-order volumes. Supplier pricing. Procurement cost analysis. Inventory intelligence Current stock levels. Low-stock products. Excess inventory. Slow-moving products. Stock distribution across warehouses. Supplier intelligence On-time delivery. Order fulfillment. Quality performance. Supplier lead times. Sales intelligence Product demand. Revenue trends. Sales performance. Order fulfillment. Warehouse intelligence Receiving and dispatch. Stock transfers. Inventory movement. Warehouse-level stock distribution. All these areas will use standardized datasets stored in a centralized AWS data lake. 3. Designing the AWS Architecture The architecture follows a layered data lake approach. Business data arrives from different systems, is stored in Amazon S3, transformed using AWS Glue, governed through AWS Lake Formation, queried with Amazon Athena, and presented through Amazon QuickSight. AWS Step Functions coordinates processing workflows, while AWS Lambda supports lightweight event-driven operations. Architecture overview BUSINESS DATA SOURCES ERP Procurement Inventory | | | +-------------+----------------+ | Sales / Suppliers / Warehouse Systems | v DATA INGESTION APIs / CSV / JSON / DB | v AMAZON S3 LANDING / RAW | v AWS GLUE ETL Clean and Transform | v AMAZON S3 CLEANSED / SILVER | v AWS GLUE ETL Business Transformations | v AMAZON S3 ANALYTICS / GOLD | +------+------+ | | v v Glue Catalog Lake Formation | Governance +------+------+ | v AMAZON ATHENA SQL Analytics | v AMAZON QUICKSIGHT Dashboards | v BUSINESS DECISIONS This is a reference architecture. The actual ingestion method and processing frequency depend on source systems and business requirements. 4. Amazon S3: The Foundation of the Data Lake Amazon S3 provides centralized storage for the platform. We can organize the data into three logical layers: smart-supply-chain-platform/ │ ├── landing/ │ ├── erp/ │ ├── procurement/ │ ├── inventory/ │ ├── sales/ │ ├── suppliers/ │ └── warehouse/ │ ├── cleansed/ │ ├── products/ │ ├── purchase_orders/ │ ├── inventory/ │ ├── sales/ │ ├── suppliers/ │ └── warehouses/ │ └── analytics/ ├── fact_inventory/ ├── fact_purchases/ ├── fact_sales/ ├── fact_deliveries/ ├── dim_products/ ├── dim_suppliers/ ├── dim_warehouses/ └── dim_date/ This follows the medallion architecture concept. Bronze: Landing or Raw Stores original source data with minimal modification. This provides traceability and allows data to be reprocessed when transformation logic changes. Silver: Cleansed Contains standardized and validated datasets. Typical operations include: Standardizing product and supplier identifiers. Handling missing values. Correcting date formats. Validating data types. Identifying duplicate records. Gold: Analytics Contains curated datasets designed for reporting and business analysis. For analytical workloads, Apache Parquet is a useful storage format because it is columnar and works well with Amazon Athena. We can also partition datasets based on common query patterns: analytics/fact_purchases/ year=2026/ month=10/ part-0001.parquet Good partitioning can reduce unnecessary data scanning. However, too many small partitions or files can hurt performance. 5. AWS Glue: Transforming Raw Data into Business Information Data from different business systems rarely follows the same structure. One system might identify a product as PROD-1001 , while another uses 1001 . Supplier names, dates, currencies, column names, and data types may also differ. AWS Glue helps process these datasets and transform them into consistent structures. A Glue ETL job can: Read CSV, JSON, and other supported formats. Standardize column names and data types. Normalize product and supplier identifiers. Validate required fields. Remove or flag duplicate records. Join related datasets. Calculate business metrics. Write optimized Parquet datasets to S3. Example: Standardizing procurement data with PySpark from pyspark . sql import functions as F purchase_orders = ( spark . read . option ( "header" , True ) . csv ( "s3://smart-supply-chain-platform/landing/procurement/" ) ) cleaned_orders = ( purchase_orders . withColumnRenamed ( "PO Number" , "purchase_order_id" ) . withColumnRenamed ( "Supplier ID" , "supplier_id" ) . withColumnRenamed ( "Order Date" , "order_date" ) . withColumnRenamed ( "Total Amount" , "total_amount" ) . withColumn ( "order_date" , F . to_date ( "order_date" , "yyyy-MM-dd" ) ) .

articles.content: You get the folder the same way every time. Someone exports a few hundred images straight out of a camera or a design tool, and now they are yours to shrink before the site can use them. A bulk image compressor is the obvious answer, but it comes in two shapes, and picking the wrong one turns a ten-minute job into an afternoon. What a bulk image compressor does under the hood It takes a folder of images and re-encodes each one at a smaller size. It decodes the file, applies a quality setting or a target size, resizes it if you ask, strips metadata like EXIF, and writes out a new file. The good ones work without uploading anything, and the fast ones process dozens of files in parallel. Two things decide how good the result looks. The first is the encoder doing the work. The second is whether the tool lets you aim at a size instead of guessing a quality number. A tool that only offers a quality slider leaves you checking file sizes by hand after every run, and that checking is where the afternoon goes. When the command line wins The command line wins when the job repeats. If you compress images every week, or the same folder gets rebuilt on every deploy, a script beats a drag-and-drop window. You write the command once, save it, and the next run takes seconds. That repeatability is the whole argument, and for a scheduled job there is no real contest. ImageMagick handles the common case in one line: mogrify -resize 1600x1600 -quality 80 -strip *.jpg That resizes every JPEG to fit inside 1600 pixels, re-encodes at quality 80, and strips the metadata. One warning: mogrify overwrites your files in place, so copy the folder first. I learned that the polite way, by reading the docs, and I would rather you learn it from this sentence than from a missing original. For a pipeline that needs more control, a short Node script with sharp does the same job and plugs into a build step: const sharp = require ( 'sharp' ) ; const fs = require ( 'fs' ) ; for ( const file of fs . readdirSync ( './photos' ) ) { sharp ( `./photos/${file}` ) . resize ( 1600 ) . jpeg ( { quality : 80 } ) . toFile ( `./web/${file}` ) ; } That script is boring, and boring is the point. It runs the same way on every deploy, and it fails loudly instead of silently producing files at the wrong size. When a bulk image compressor in the browser wins The browser wins when the job is a one-off and the folder is already on your machine. You open the page, drop the files in, set a size, and download the results. There is nothing to install, nothing to update, and no script to debug. For a folder you will touch once, skipping setup is the entire point. The other advantage is privacy, with one condition: the tool has to process files locally. SnapShrink's bulk image compressor runs the whole job in your browser, so the files never leave your machine. A server-side uploader is a different deal, and for client photos or unreleased product shots, that difference matters. If you only need one image under an exact limit instead of a whole folder, the main compressor takes a target size in kilobytes and aims at that number directly. How to pick in thirty seconds Four questions settle the choice, and you can answer them before you open any tool. Frequency matters most: a job you repeat deserves a script, and a job you do once deserves the fastest path to done. Volume, privacy, and repeatability fill in the rest, and together they point at one of the two routes without much debate. Privacy deserves a note of its own. A browser tool that processes files locally and a CLI tool both keep your images on your machine. A server-side uploader sends them somewhere else, and for client work that distinction is worth checking before you drag a folder in. What can go wrong Most batch compression regret comes from a few mistakes, and all of them are easy to avoid. Overwriting originals tops the list. Resizing without keeping the aspect ratio produces stretched images. Forgetting to strip metadata is the quiet one: a phone photo can carry location data, and that data survives compression unless you remove it. A dry run on three files catches all of these. Compress a small sample, check the sizes, open one image at full size, and confirm the originals are still where you left them. The whole check takes two minutes, and it is the cheapest insurance in this workflow. A workflow that uses both Most teams end up using both routes, and that is the sensible outcome rather than a failure to decide. The build pipeline gets a script, because deploys should never depend on someone remembering to compress images. The one-off folder from a client gets the browser tool, because scripting a job you will do once wastes a good afternoon. Questions I hear about batch compression The same three questions come up every time I write about this, so here are the short answers. The details above cover the how; these cover the worries people have before they run a batch job on files they care about. Does batch compression reduce quality? Yes, if you use lossy settings, and no, if you only resize or strip metadata. Quality 80 JPEG looks the same as the original to most eyes on a screen. Keep a copy of the originals either way, because you cannot get quality back once it is gone. Can I compress images without uploading them? Yes. A browser tool that processes files locally never sends them anywhere, and a CLI tool never touches a network at all.

articles.summary: A bulk image compressor shrinks folders of images by re-encoding files, applying quality settings, resizing, and stripping metadata. Two main options exist: command-line tools like ImageMagick and Node's sharp for repeatable jobs, and browser-based tools like SnapShrink for one-off tasks. CLI tools excel for weekly compressions or deploy pipelines, offering scriptability and parallel processing. Browser tools provide instant results with no installation when processing files locally. The choice depends on frequency, volume, privacy needs, and repeatability, with most teams using both routes for different scenarios.

articles.content: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub. Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins. You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan. Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together. Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately. Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions. Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation. What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan. Build: Move more than one task forward at a time You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time. You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it. Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you. Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes , keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later. Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree. Carry project knowledge into each task. Repository instructions capture conventions and validation commands, while shared memory stores useful facts Copilot can reuse across a repository. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible sessions and pull request feedback to keep memories current and propose instruction or skill updates. That means less time re-explaining how your team works and more consistent help from Copilot across tasks. Match the models to the work. Select Copilot Fusion to choose models and reasoning depth for the task, bringing in additional models to review a solution when needed. You set the effort level to balance quality, cost, and response time. Follow company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your company’s policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces, reducing setup differences as you move between clients. Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review. Verify: Spend your attention where it counts After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board. That review queue is the 441% in practice.

articles.content: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens , which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others , are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today. Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day. This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost . But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures. What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography. One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance. One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer. Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product. However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate. This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement . An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator . Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set , the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site. An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it.

articles.content:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates . I run an automated monitoring pipeline that watches Carousell for newly-listed items and pings me on Telegram when something fresh appears. It is one container on my Synology NAS, driven through Portainer, with a single Python process as PID 1 on a Docker bridge network. One day it stopped pinging. The container was healthy, the scraper was still archiving listings into NocoDB — but every notification died with the same three characters in the log: telegram sendPhoto failed: 400 ... nginx/1.30.1 That string, nginx/1.30.1 , became the villain of a day-long debugging session. This is the story of how a deceptively small bug turned out to be three separate problems stacked on top of each other — and how I'd find each one faster next time. The problem The bot had two jobs: collect listings, and notify me. Collection worked. Notification didn't. The log said 400 Bad Request and pointed at a server identifying itself as nginx/1.30.1 . My first assumption was textbook: something in the network is intercepting the request. nginx/1.30.1 is not a header I associated with Telegram's API. A 400 with an HTML body (Telegram returns JSON even on errors) smelled like a local reverse proxy or a VPN gateway rejecting traffic before it ever left the machine. Assumptions like that are cheap. They're also wrong a lot. Let me walk through what I actually found. What I tried, and why each thing failed Round 1: it must be DNS / IPv6 I checked getMe from inside the container. It worked. Then I checked sendMessage . It failed. Same token, same container, one method up, one down. The giveaway was in how the two endpoints resolved: # inside the container $ getent hosts api.telegram.org 2001:67c:4e8:f004::9 api.telegram.org The container resolved api.telegram.org to IPv6 only — a single AAAA record and no A record. The container ran on a Docker bridge network with no IPv6 connectivity . So every request that needed api.telegram.org was trying to reach an IPv6 address it had no route to. The fix looked obvious: pin the IPv4 address with extra_hosts . I did, and the DNS answer became exactly what I expected: 149.154.167.220 api.telegram.org And the notifications still failed. Same 400. My proud fix did nothing. Round 2: I picked the wrong IP Here's a mistake worth remembering: I hard-coded 149.154.167.220 from memory. When I finally queried a public resolver, the real A record for api.telegram.org was different: 149.154.166.110 api.telegram.org # what DNS actually says 149.154.167.220 api.telegram.org # what I hard-coded 167.220 is inside Telegram's IP range ( 149.154.160.0/20 ), so it's not "wrong" in the sense of being somebody else's server — but it's not the active endpoint, and bot-API traffic to it behaved unpredictably. I switched to 166.110 . It still failed. So the IP wasn't the whole story either. Round 3: the same command, two different outcomes This was the moment the whole thing got weird. Inside one container, at almost the same second: the long-running monitor process ( PID 1 ) → sendPhoto failed, 400 a fresh docker exec process running identical code → sendPhoto succeeded, 200 Same container. Same code. Same payload. Same second. I ruled out token, chat_id, emoji in the caption, Unicode quotes, image format, environment variables, and the image URL itself — I download-tested the photo and it was a perfectly valid JPEG. Nothing in the code differed between the two paths. When you hit a contradiction like that — "identical inputs, opposite outputs" — the answer is usually that the inputs aren't identical. In my docker exec test, I had tested against a lightweight sample image; but the PID 1 loop was processing real scraped listing photos where binary byte sequences happened to break multipart boundary parsing. The binary payloads were not the same. But finding the difference took one more frame change. Round 4: nginx/1.30.1 is Telegram I re-read the raw 400 response instead of assuming. The response was an HTML "400 Bad Request" page, and the Server header was nginx/1.30.1 . That nginx is Telegram's own edge. Telegram's API sits behind nginx (version 1.30.1), and when a request is malformed before it reaches their application layer, nginx itself answers with a plain 400 page — no JSON, no friendly error code. That reframed everything. The request wasn't being intercepted. It was reaching Telegram, and Telegram's nginx was rejecting it as malformed. And the malformed thing was the one part I hadn't scrutinized: the sendPhoto multipart body. The fix My original helper assembled the multipart body by treating headers and binary payloads as a list of "lines" and joining them with b"
".join(body_lines) — the kind of "obviously fine" shortcut that ships a framing bug: # BROKEN: pre-terminated chunks or line-split binary data re-joined with b"
" body = b "
" . join ( body_lines ) It fails in two ways, and neither is bytes.join() rewriting the JPEG — b"
".join() only inserts the delimiter between list elements and never touches bytes inside an element. The damage happens upstream. First, if the payload ever passes through line-oriented handling such as .splitlines() , every lone 0x0D or 0x0A byte inside the compressed image stream is treated as a line break and rewritten to 
 , which mutates the JPEG and desynchronises the Content-Length that was computed from the original file. Second, if any chunk in body_lines already carries its own trailing 
 , the join adds a second one, so the body reads --boundary

Content-Disposition: ... — and in MIME framing a blank line terminates the part headers, so that part becomes an anonymous body whose first line is the Content-Disposition header. Telegram's edge nginx/1.30.1 rejects that as malformed with an HTML 400 long before the Bot API parses anything. That also closes the Round 3 contradiction.
