articles.title: Why Telegram Bot Notifications Die: IPv6, DNS, and a 400 That Took a Day
articles.headline: Telegram bot notifications fail due to IPv6 routing and multipart framing bug
articles.summary:
A monitoring pipeline on Synology NAS stopped sending Telegram notifications despite healthy containers. Debugging revealed three stacked issues: the container resolved Telegram's API to IPv6 with no connectivity, a hardcoded IP address was incorrect, and the multipart body framing used b'
'.join() which corrupted image bytes and added duplicate line endings. Telegram's edge nginx/1.30.1 rejected the malformed request with a 400 error. The fix involved correcting DNS routing, using b''.join() for byte concatenation, and downloading images locally before upload.

articles.content: A fee comparison showed a price that was wrong for about six minutes every night, and only for some exchanges. Not stale, not missing — wrong. The kind of wrong that makes a user screenshot it and ask why your numbers do not match the exchange's own page. The cause was not the price feed. It was the day boundary. Every exchange resets on its own midnight Trading fee tiers are usually computed per rolling period, but several exchanges reset allowances and volume counters on a calendar day in the exchange's local time . So the question "what is my fee tier right now" depends on what time it is where the exchange's accounting lives, not where the user is and not where your server is. An aggregator that normalises everything to UTC — which is the correct instinct for storage — quietly moves that boundary. For an exchange at UTC+8, the tier resets at 16:00 UTC. If your code resets at 00:00 UTC, then between 16:00 and 24:00 UTC you are computing today's tier against yesterday's volume, and the fee you display is off by whatever the tier step is. Six minutes was not the error window. Six minutes was how long it took someone to notice. Three timestamp shapes, one of them a trap The same normalisation bug shows up in three forms, and only the third is obvious: Epoch milliseconds. Unambiguous. Convert and move on. ISO 8601 with an offset ( 2026-11-11T09:00:00+08:00 ). Unambiguous if you keep the offset. ISO 8601 without an offset ( 2026-11-11T09:00:00 ). This is the trap. Every parser will assume something — server local, UTC, or browser local — and all three assumptions are wrong for at least one exchange. The string looks like a timestamp and behaves like a guess. If you parse shape 3 with a default timezone, you get a value that is correct in one environment and wrong in another. That is the worst failure mode available: it passes local tests and fails in production, or passes in production and fails after a deploy moves the container's TZ . Store the exchange's clock, not just the instant The fix that held up was to stop treating time as a single instant and store two things: the instant , in UTC, for ordering and display; the exchange's local date , as a plain YYYY-MM-DD string, for anything that resets on a day boundary. The second field is what makes tier logic testable. You are no longer asking "what time is it", you are asking "which of the exchange's days does this belong to", and that question has one answer regardless of where the code runs. def exchange_day ( ts_utc : datetime , tz : ZoneInfo ) -> date : """The calendar date the exchange would print on a statement.""" return ts_utc . astimezone ( tz ) . date ( ) Two lines, and it removes an entire class of bug — the one where the same input produces different output depending on the machine. Test the boundary, not the middle The test that would have caught this is not "does the fee match for a sample trade". It is: freeze the clock at 23:59 exchange-local and assert tier A; freeze it at 00:01 exchange-local and assert tier B; run both with TZ=UTC , TZ=Asia/Shanghai and TZ=America/New_York . If the answers differ between the three runs, you have a timezone dependency in business logic, and it will surface as a support ticket at the worst possible hour. If they agree, you have actually fixed it rather than moved it. The same discipline applies to rounding, which has the same shape of problem — the value is fine, the rule about when to apply it is what breaks. Rounding is a business rule, not a formatting detail , and it fails in the same quiet way: correct on the happy path, wrong at the edge, invisible until someone adds up a month of trades. Cache the answer, but not the boundary One more thing worth saying, because it is how this bug survived a deploy: the tier was cached. The cache key was the exchange and the account, with a TTL of an hour. That is a perfectly reasonable cache — and it made the bug persist for up to an hour after the real value changed. If a value has a day-boundary dependency, the boundary belongs in the cache key, not just the TTL. Otherwise the cache outlives the fact. The general case for rarely-changing data is the same problem in slower motion : a TTL is a guess about when data changes, and a guessed boundary is a bug waiting for the one day it matters. None of this is exotic. It is the ordinary cost of aggregating numbers that other people computed under assumptions they never wrote down. The exchanges are not wrong to reset on their own day; we were wrong to assume they reset on ours. If you want to see what the output looks like when the boundaries are handled correctly, the comparison this work feeds is at fipst.com — the tier figures there are computed in exchange-local time, and the timestamps carry the offset they were computed with.
articles.excerpt: A fee comparison showed a price that was wrong for about six minutes every night, and only for some exchanges. Not stale, not missing — wrong. The kind of wrong that makes a user screenshot it and ask why your numbers do not match the exchange's own page. The cause was not the price feed.
articles.title: Time zones are the bug: a price feed that is wrong at midnight
articles.headline: Price tiers wrong at midnight due to timezone bug
articles.summary: A price feed showed incorrect fee tiers for about six minutes each night due to timezone handling. Exchanges reset fee allowances on their local midnight, but an aggregator normalizing to UTC 00:00 created a mismatch. For exchanges at UTC+8, the tier resets at 16:00 UTC, causing incorrect fee calculations between 16:00 and 24:00 UTC. The bug stems from parsing ISO 8601 timestamps without timezone offsets, leading to inconsistent assumptions. The fix requires storing both UTC instant and the exchange's local date for day-boundary logic.

articles.content: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture. The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components. Building for agent scale We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes: Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few. Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis. Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes. We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then. We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to: Accept thousands of writes per second. Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this: Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly. Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails. Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step. Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request. Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio. Let each component scale independently. On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally. Introducing “Project Rubicon” In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development. Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new. Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency.
articles.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
articles.headline: GitHub announces new storage architecture capable of 7,200 pushes per second
articles.summary: GitHub unveiled its new Git storage architecture at GitHub Universe, designed to support thousands of concurrent agents writing to repositories. Internal testing demonstrated the system can handle 7,200 pushes per second with consistently low read latency. The architecture decouples storage from compute and minimizes coordination, allowing reference updates to scale independently. This foundation aims to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers while maintaining Git's familiar workflow.

articles.content: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries . An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle : The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. The intermediary problem Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business. Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra. Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra. None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today. A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents. In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost . That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved. Our vision Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification. None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action.
articles.excerpt: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users.
articles.title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
articles.headline: Cloudflare warns AI agents could eclipse human browsing, breaking site accountability
articles.summary: Cloudflare argues AI agents acting on the web for millions of users break site accountability by removing identity and reputation signals. As agent traffic grows, sites lose the ability to distinguish individual users, enforce age/geographic rules, prevent friendly fraud, or monetize content, as they can only see the agent, not the user behind it. The post calls for new mechanisms to preserve the user-site relationship as agentic traffic may soon eclipse traditional browsing.

articles.content: STATERA Library · Series 02 · Volume 11 · Chapter 23 · KR Source: https://github.com/Statera-Library/02_Vol_11_Differential_Drive_Steer_Drive_and_Omni_Drive/blob/main/23_Steer_Drive_Power_and_Electrical_System/23_Steer_Drive_Power_and_Electrical_System_KR.md 01 48 V vs 72 V selection 01 48V vs 72V Selection 1.1 Voltage Decision Factor Analysis 1.2 48V Peak Current 104A Analysis Under Sequential Operation 1.3 Conditions Requiring 72V and Trade-offs 1.1 전압 결정 요소 분석 (Voltage Decision Factor Analysis) 적절한 시스템 전압(System Voltage)을 선택하는 것은 자율주행 이동로봇(Autonomous Mobile Robot, AMR)의 전기 아키텍처(Electrical Architecture)를 설계할 때 가장 중요한 의사결정 가운데 하나이다. 현재 산업용 이동로봇에서는 48V 와 72V 배터리 시스템이 모두 널리 사용되고 있지만, 최적의 전압은 단순히 모터 출력(Motor Power)만으로 결정되지 않는다. 시스템 전압은 배터리 구성(Battery Configuration), 인버터 효율(Inverter Efficiency), 케이블 규격(Cable Sizing), 열관리(Thermal Management), 안전성(Safety), 충전 시스템(Charging Infrastructure), 부품 수급(Component Availability), 유지보수(Maintenance), 그리고 향후 플랫폼 확장성(Platform Scalability)까지 전체 차량 설계에 영향을 미친다. 따라서 시스템 전압은 단순한 전기 계산이 아니라 시스템 전체(System-level Optimization)를 고려하여 결정해야 한다. 가장 먼저 고려해야 하는 요소는 전력 전달 효율(Power Transmission Efficiency) 이다. 전력(Power)은 전압(Voltage)과 전류(Current)의 곱으로 결정된다. 동일한 전력을 전달할 경우 전압이 높아질수록 필요한 전류는 감소한다. 전류가 감소하면 도체 저항에 의한 손실은 I²R 법칙(I²R Relationship) 에 따라 크게 줄어든다. 즉 전류가 조금만 감소해도 케이블 발열(Cable Heating), 커넥터 온도 상승(Connector Temperature Rise), 인버터 도통 손실(Conduction Loss)이 크게 감소한다. 따라서 지속적으로 높은 출력을 사용하는 시스템에서는 일반적으로 높은 전압이 더 높은 전기 효율(Electrical Efficiency)을 제공한다. 그러나 효율만이 전압을 결정하는 기준은 아니다. 대부분의 산업용 AMR은 최대 출력(Maximum Power)으로 계속 운행하지 않는다. 실제 운전에서는 추진 모터(Propulsion Motor)가 부분 부하(Partial Load) 상태로 동작하는 시간이 훨씬 길며, 가속과 감속은 매우 짧은 시간 동안만 발생한다. 또한 조향(Steering), 위치 제어(Position Control), 센서(Sensor) 및 컴퓨팅 장치(Computing System)는 각각 다른 부하 특성을 가진다. 따라서 순간 최대 출력(Peak Power)만을 기준으로 시스템을 설계하면 실제 운행 조건보다 훨씬 과도한 용량의 전기 시스템이 구성되어 비용, 무게, 복잡성만 증가할 수 있다. 부품의 공급성(Component Availability) 역시 매우 중요한 요소이다. 현재 산업 시장에서는 48V 배터리, 모터 컨트롤러(Motor Controller), DC/DC 컨버터(DC/DC Converter), 접촉기(Contactor), 배터리 관리 시스템(Battery Management System, BMS), 충전기(Charger), 안전 장치(Safety Device) 등 매우 다양한 제품이 표준화되어 있다. 전동 지게차(Electric Forklift), AGV, 서비스 로봇(Service Robot), 통신 장비(Telecommunication Equipment), 에너지 저장 시스템(Energy Storage System) 등에서 오랫동안 사용되어 왔기 때문에 생산량이 많고 가격 경쟁력이 높으며 기술 지원도 풍부하다. 반면 72V 제품은 존재하지만 상대적으로 특수 시장(Specialized Market)에 사용되기 때문에 공급업체가 적고 가격도 높은 편이다. 안전성(Safety) 측면에서도 48V는 장점이 있다. 48V와 72V 모두 적절한 보호 회로가 필요하지만, 48V는 많은 국제 규격에서 위험 저전압(Hazardous Extra-Low Voltage) 기준 이하로 분류되는 경우가 많다. 따라서 절연(Insulation) 요구사항이 비교적 단순하고, 커넥터 설계가 쉬우며, 유지보수 시 감전(Electric Shock)의 위험도 낮다. 결과적으로 안전 인증(Safety Certification)과 유지보수 교육도 상대적으로 단순해질 수 있다. 열관리(Thermal Management) 도 중요한 결정 요소이다. 72V는 동일 출력에서 전류가 감소하므로 케이블 단면적(Cable Cross Section)을 줄일 수 있고 발열도 감소한다. 그러나 대부분의 산업용 AMR은 최대 출력으로 지속 운행하지 않기 때문에 실제 열관리 측면에서의 차이는 예상보다 크지 않은 경우가 많다. 적절한 케이블 규격과 고효율 전력전자(Power Electronics), 그리고 스마트 전류 관리(Current Management)를 적용하면 48V 시스템도 산업용 열관리 요구사항을 충분히 만족할 수 있다. 배터리 구조(Battery Architecture) 역시 전압 선택에 영향을 준다. 48V 리튬인산철 배터리(Lithium Iron Phosphate, LFP)는 72V보다 직렬 연결되는 셀(Cell)의 개수가 적다. 셀 수가 적으면 BMS 설계가 단순해지고 셀 밸런싱(Cell Balancing)이 쉬워지며 제조 공정도 단순해진다. 또한 장기간 사용 시 셀 간 불균형(Cell Mismatch) 발생 가능성도 감소한다. 유지보수와 배터리 교체 역시 보다 간단하게 수행할 수 있다. 반면 확장성(Scalability) 도 함께 고려해야 한다. 향후 더 큰 적재 중량(Payload), 더 높은 주행 속도(Travel Speed), 더 많은 보조 장치(Auxiliary Equipment)를 사용할 계획이라면 48V의 실질적인 한계에 도달할 수 있다. 따라서 현재는 48V를 사용하더라도 향후 72V로 쉽게 확장할 수 있는 모듈형 전기 인터페이스(Modular Electrical Interface)를 설계하는 것이 장기적인 플랫폼 경쟁력 확보에 도움이 된다. 결국 시스템 전압은 단순한 전기 계산이 아니라 실제 운행 시나리오(Mission Profile)를 기준으로 결정해야 한다. 적절한 순차 운전(Sequential Operation), 스마트 전력 관리(Intelligent Power Management), 산업용 적재 중량을 사용하는 대부분의 AMR에서는 성숙한 48V 시스템이 우수한 성능을 제공한다. 반면 지속적인 고출력 운전, 대형 차량, 향후 플랫폼 확장성이 중요한 경우에는 72V 시스템이 더 적합할 수 있다. 1.2 순차 운전(Sequential Operation) 조건에서 48V 최대 전류 104A 분석 (48V Peak Current 104A Analysis Under Sequential Operation) 48V 시스템을 설계할 때 가장 자주 제기되는 질문 가운데 하나는 여러 전기 장치가 동시에 동작하면 전류(Current)가 너무 커지는 것이 아닌가 하는 점이다. 추진 모터, 조향 모터, 산업용 컴퓨터(Industrial Computer), LiDAR, 카메라(Camera), 통신 장비(Communication Equipment), 배터리 관리 시스템(BMS), 보조 장치(Auxiliary Device) 등을 모두 합산하면 매우 큰 전류가 필요한 것처럼 보인다. 그러나 실제 산업용 AMR은 이러한 모든 장치가 동시에 최대 출력으로 동작하는 경우가 거의 없으며, 대부분 순차 운전(Sequential Operation) 방식을 사용하여 부하를 분산시킨다. 순차 운전은 현대 AMR의 전력 관리(Power Management)의 핵심 개념이다. 제어기(Motion Controller)는 모든 액추에이터(Actuator)를 동시에 최대 출력으로 동작시키지 않고, 주요 부하가 서로 다른 시점에 발생하도록 제어한다. 예를 들어 차량이 가속할 때는 추진 모터가 우선적으로 큰 출력을 사용하며, 조향 동작은 대부분 그 직전에 완료된다. 일정 속도로 주행하는 동안에는 추진 모터의 부하는 크게 감소하고, 조향 모터는 방향을 변경할 때만 순간적으로 동작한다. 정밀 도킹 단계에서는 추진 출력은 매우 낮아지고 조향 정밀도가 더욱 중요해진다. 따라서 실제 운행에서는 모든 장치의 최대 전류가 동시에 발생하지 않는다. 예를 들어 48V 기반 산업용 AMR을 생각해 보면, 급가속 시에는 추진 모터가 높은 전류를 소비하지만 조향 모터는 방향을 변경하는 짧은 시간 동안만 동작한다. 목표 조향각에 도달하면 유지 토크(Holding Torque)는 매우 작아진다. 반면 산업용 컴퓨터, LiDAR, 카메라, 통신 장치, 안전 제어기(Safety Controller)는 차량 가속 여부와 관계없이 거의 일정한 전력을 소비한다. 따라서 이들 장치는 순간 최대 전류 증가에 미치는 영향이 제한적이다. 이러한 순차 운전을 적용하면 약 104A 수준의 최대 전류(Peak Current) 는 48V 시스템에서도 충분히 현실적인 수준이다. 이러한 최대 전류는 매우 짧은 시간 동안만 발생하며, 연속 운전(Continuous Operation)에서는 훨씬 낮은 평균 전류(Average Current)가 흐른다. 적절한 방전 성능을 가진 리튬인산철 배터리는 이러한 순간 방전(Peak Discharge)을 충분히 지원할 수 있으며, 배터리 전압도 안정적으로 유지할 수 있다. 현대의 LFP 배터리는 연속 방전 전류보다 훨씬 높은 순간 방전 전류를 허용하는 경우가 많아 추가적인 안전 여유(Safety Margin)를 제공한다. 배터리 관리 시스템(BMS) 은 이러한 운용을 더욱 안전하게 만든다. BMS는 전류(Current), 전압(Voltage), 온도(Temperature), 셀 밸런싱(Cell Balancing), 방전 한계(Discharge Limit)를 지속적으로 감시한다. 만약 과도한 부하가 발생하면 차량 가속을 일시적으로 제한하거나, 일부 장치의 동작을 순차적으로 조정하거나, 중요한 시스템에 우선적으로 전력을 공급하는 방식으로 배터리를 보호한다. 모터 컨트롤러(Motor Controller) 역시 전류 제한(Current Limiting) 기능을 제공한다. 서보 드라이브(Servo Drive)는 무제한 전류를 허용하지 않고 배터리 상태, 온도, 모터 특성, 차량 견인력(Traction)에 따라 토크를 자동으로 제한한다.

articles.content: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work. Accessibility statements make project practices visible GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement , for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes. The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are. The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations. The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation. Document what the project can maintain There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current. Priorities and goals: Explain why accessibility matters to the project and which user experiences receive attention. Contributor expectations: Describe the accessibility checks, evidence, or review practices expected for changes, including instructions for human contributors and coding agents. Reporting accessibility barriers: Provide a direct, accessible reporting path. Do not require disability disclosure, screenshots, or recordings. Response process: Explain how maintainers acknowledge, triage, track, and communicate about accessibility issues. If the project uses severity levels, let maintainers assign or confirm them during triage. Supported environments: List the platforms, browsers, input methods, and assistive technologies the project supports or has tested. Known limitations: Describe barriers in terms of the affected experience, include available workarounds, and link to tracked remediation work. Ownership and maintenance: Name the team, role, or maintainer responsible for keeping the statement and related practices current. Feedback and improvements: Explain how users and contributors can suggest changes to the statement or the project’s accessibility practices. Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator. What the most useful ACCESSIBILITY.md files contain The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language. Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability. The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix. Start with an example and adapt it The Open Source Accessibility Toolkit provides a detailed public example. GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature. Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work. Add an accessibility statement to your repository >

articles.content: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. See how agents access your site Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants. Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it. Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block. Set access policies that reflect your preferences We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies . In Security Settings , you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block) , Block on pages with ads , or Block . For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads , then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are. You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings . The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business. Agent identity is only part of the story The analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply. Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users. Make the choice for your site That person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

articles.title: See the agents, set the terms: New visibility and control for personal agents
articles.headline: Cloudflare launches analytics and access controls for personal agents

Site owners can set granular access policies for individual supported personal agents, choosing to allow or block them based on site needs. The updates include visibility into which agents visit, their request patterns, and which user accounts they represent, enabling more informed decisions about agent access while preserving user context.

articles.content: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation

articles.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
articles.headline: Claude Fable 5.2 adds code based on ownership prompts
articles.summary: Anthropic testing found Claude Fable 5.2 modifies code structure based on ownership prompts. When prompts claimed code as someone else's, the model added to existing structure. When told the codebase was its own, the model merged repeated code in about half of tries, compared to under a tenth without the prompt. This behavior affects how the model handles code improvement tasks.

articles.content: Before we start, I’d like to share some exciting news: The Pragmatic Summit is returning! It’s a one-day event on 10 February in San Francisco, almost exactly one year after the first Summit. I’ll be hosting and the first few speakers are confirmed. Some faces may be familiar to regular readers and listeners! My goal with the Summit is to make it the single best event for connecting with like-minded engineering leaders and engineers, and curious, driven people. Feedback from last year was that it was the attendees and the quality of debate that made it a standout event. We aim to deliver the same this time with the organizing team, including space for roundtable discussions, and talking with speakers who can stay around after their talk. The Pragmatic Engineer team shall be there too. Applications are open : this summit is for senior+ engineers and engineering leaders who are shaping how modern engineering teams build software, ship products, and scale up to meet challenging demand curves. Tickets are priced at $1,000. You can check out last year’s talks , or watch a one-minute video summary. This year’s Summit is made possible by friends at WorkOS , which is helping organize the event and is the exclusive sponsor. Thank you! I hope to see many of you there! Now, onto today’s article. Sean Allen is a software engineer with deep expertise in building large distributed systems, stream processing, and confidential computing. He is a core contributor to the programming language Pony , which is designed for concurrency. Sean is a distinguished engineer at Antithesis. I was keen to talk with Sean due to his work on confidential computing at Microsoft, as well as his extensive work on the Pony language, and his passion for software correctness, which he works on fulltime at Antithesis. For this conversation, we set ourselves the challenge of discussing modern software engineering without using the phrase “AI” a single time. Read on to see if it’s possible in 2026… In this article, the questions are posed by me in bold font, with Sean’s words in normal font. Today we cover: Software correctness & languages built for correctness. Why languages in the Meta Language (ML) family that are built around strong type systems catch more errors during compilation time than those in the Algorithmic Language (ALGOL) family. Does anybody care about testing? For someone passionate about correctness, Sean is surprisingly anti-testing. He argues that manual testing is the worst way to ensure correctness because you want illegal states to be prohibited from being expressed in a language – even before testing. Workloads & correctness. A more robust way of testing stuff than things like unit tests, is to define “workloads” that can be executed numerous times during a test. A common workload example is The Bank Test to stress test database isolation guarantees. Is quality a “gate” or not? It’s tempting to think of quality checks as closed gates that keep out poor quality. Sean pushes back against this; he says it’s important to consider quality from the very start, and to build with validation techniques that provide feedback on correctness. He prefers this to adding CI/CD quality “gates” late in the development process. Tech debt only hurts if you have to pay it back. Stop being afraid of tech debt because you often don’t need to pay it back at all! Sean says it’s common that tech debt is disregarded during rewrites when a system has become popular. No good fix for supply chain security. Supply chain attacks – when a package gets hijacked by an attacker and malicious code is executed on a machine or service – are very hard to defend against because languages with truly robust defenses, like ‘E’, are unpopular, while popular languages assume a trustworthy ecosystem. There’s no single or simple fix, says Sean. Garbage collection is slow – but doesn’t have to be. A summary of why garbage collection is devastating for runtime performance, and how Sean built a predictably performant approach in the Pony language. Go slow to go fast. Counter-intuitive advice: spend more time designing upfront and aligning everyone, and then you’ll move fast! You can also watch this conversation on YouTube : An amusing detail: Sean and I discovered we share in common a first fulltime employer. We both worked at a company called ‘Sense/Net’ at the start of our careers, although they were totally separate businesses in different countries. The founders of each must’ve been fans of the foundational cyberpunk novel, ‘Neuromancer’ by William Gibson, where the ‘Sense/Net’ name comes from . Note: Antithesis is a podcast sponsor, but this deepdive is not sponsored by them. I’ve just been thinking a lot more about software correctness in the context of AI agents producing more code than ever, thereby creating opportunities for more bugs to ship to prod than ever. I wanted to learn more about this from an engineer with extensive experience in this area. 1. Software correctness & languages built for correctness Gergely: How do you define ‘software correctness’? Sean: “It’s down to whether my program does what I expect. I tend to talk about things in terms of ‘invariants,’ which is a more formal specification term. An invariant is a guarantee that my software does what’s expected of it. But here’s the problem: in lots of cases, people don’t know what they expect their software to do upfront! They know when it’s not working, but they don’t necessarily know what it means for it to be working. ‘Correct’ software does its business purpose and doesn’t wake anybody up at 2 a.m. with an outage. That is correct enough for me.” Your personal definition of ‘beautiful code’ mirrors this. Sean: “I was on the CoRecursive podcast when the subject of beautiful code in Ruby came up. I didn’t really know what people meant when they said ‘beautiful code’.

articles.title: Software correctness & supply chain security, with Sean Allen
articles.headline: Sean Allen discusses software correctness and supply chain security at Antithesis
articles.summary: Sean Allen, a core contributor to the Pony language and distinguished engineer at Antithesis, discusses software correctness, arguing that languages with strong type systems catch more errors at compilation. He critiques manual testing, advocates for defining workloads to stress test systems, and warns that supply chain attacks are difficult to defend against in popular languages. Allen also explains how the Pony language addresses garbage collection performance and advises spending more time on upfront design to reduce technical debt.

articles.content: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

articles.content: Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior. Kiran Prakash explains durable execution: an emerging pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards their goal. In this programming model, the runtime keeps a record of the result of each step that interacts with the outside world so that, when a failure occurs, the program runs again, completed steps are skipped, and the program's state is rebuilt from the record. more…

articles.content: Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

articles.content: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep .

articles.content: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

articles.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
articles.headline: Claude Code builds Beep Locator to triangulate mysterious room beep
articles.summary: Simon Willison used Claude Code to build Beep Locator, a software system triangulating a mysterious beep using multiple browser-connected devices. The system estimates beep location within 40cm by recording audio clips and using chirp alignment. It successfully located an ancient carbon monoxide detector with dead batteries. Features include rough mode dragging, clap detection, timestamped logs, and a mystery beep confirmation button.

articles.content: Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery! As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings . On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week. AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text , while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech , we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week , including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS Presented by I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy. Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating. Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them. Stratechery Articles and Updates Google Earnings, Facebook Déjà Vu, The Agent Play — Google’s earnings miss looks a lot like Facebook’s, and that’s a credit to Google. The company is being more aggressive than they get credit for. Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression — Apple’s earnings suggest that the company’s hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt? AI on the Ballot — Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent? An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI — An interview with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi about the working for one of tech’s oldest software companies, and how Intuit is leaning into the AI paradigm shift. Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp X Marks the Rot — Republicans colonized Twitter and then cannibalized their support with two years of memes, corruption and excess. articles.content: Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – The tpuf eng team is completely redesigning their storage architecture from first principles. And they’re documenting all of it! They made epic progress; take a look: turbopuffer.com/v3 • Antithesis – use AI agents to work on critical systems without worrying about correctness. Antithesis runs your complete system in a hostile environment, analyzes its behavior, and reproduces every issue perfectly. Learn more • Entire – Entire launched its own Git forge, shipped Continuous Memory , and reinvented the pull request (called Trails ). Trails are a much more natural workflow when agents keep pushing new changes, after iterating on feedback – and you have more context and control on when a change is ready to merge. Check it out In this episode What is involved in scaling up large, popular products at places like Slack and GitHub? We get an insider’s view on this from Maude Lemaire , a principal engineer and author of ‘ Refactoring at Scale: Regaining Control of Your Codebase .’ She spent nearly eight years at Slack, where she led the backend performance infrastructure team, before joining GitHub to tackle database scaling challenges. Most recently, she worked on improving performance at Cursor – including time to first token. In this episode of The Pragmatic Engineer , Maude and I dig into the challenges of scaling some of the world’s largest software products. We explore how Slack handled growing numbers of enterprise customers, how it evolved its approach to load testing, and the lessons Maude learned during nearly eight years of scaling Slack’s infrastructure. She also tells us what it was like joining GitHub in 2024 when Copilot was taking off, the challenges of working with GitHub’s gigantic Rails monolith, and how Maude uses AI in her work – while keeping judgment calls and decision-making firmly in her own hands. Takeaways from the conversation with Maude Here are eight interesting points from our discussion: 1. Performance should matter even if there’s no competition. In 2015, the homepage of Rent the Runway took up to 10 seconds to fully load due to a high-resolution hero image on the site. Maude was told it wasn’t an issue because there were no competitors to worry about. She thought differently: “The best competition is competition with yourself, knowing that you can do better, knowing that you can drive a better experience, ” she said. Maude spent some free time on speeding up the website without asking for permission to do so because it was the right call. 2. Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid thundering herds. Here’s an example of a thundering herd : the CEO of a 100,000-member Slack channel posts “everyone gets Friday off!” In response, people start posting custom emojis – hundreds of them. The problem is that every single custom emoji has to fan out to all 100,000 users. With 10 custom emojis, that’s 1,000,000 fan-outs, with 100 it’s 10,000,000; a lot of network load! Slack limits custom emojis to 23 to avoid this problem. In reality, the absent 24th custom emoji is not missed. 3. Event floods can cripple the machines of Slack’s power users. Event floods are the cousin of thundering herds: they occur when a single client is overwhelmed by events coming through its own WebSocket. For example, when an IT worker is logged into lots of busy channels and they all receive the “everyone gets Friday off!” message – along with all the associated custom emojis and messages. This “power user” gets a sudden influx of messages with no deduplication and they struggle. 4. Load testing 500,000 WebSocket connections the simple way would have cost $150,000 per run. A new customer with 500,000 users was about to sign up to Slack, and Maude needed to run a load test to confirm the service could handle the load. Initially, she planned to spin up headless Chrome instances – each instance running a Slack session, and that would have cost $0.37 per five-hour session, per instance. The total price would’ve been crazily expensive. Instead, Maude built a tool called Koi Pond that spins up slimmed-down versions of Slack (‘Koi’), written in Go to establish the WebSocket connections. 5. Active Record downside: too much database load! GitHub used to be a Ruby on Rails monolith, which used Active Record as a database abstraction layer. This caused unexpected load: GitHub’s home page fetched live data from the database for most reloads, and loading the home page regularly triggered 100 SQL queries across three database clusters. This revealed a downside of abstractions like Active Record to Maude: when devs used it, they didn’t know or care about the additional load they unwittingly placed on the database while fetching data for whatever they were working on. 6. GitHub could not add more than 16 database shards because of scatter query problems. A scatter query is one without a primary key (a sharding key), and it needs to be run across all shard instances . But more shards make such queries slower. Back in the day at GitHub, lots of queries made through Active Record (many on the homepage) were scatter queries. This limitation prevented GitHub from adding more than 16 shards. I find this detail fascinating: it shows why a developer-friendly abstraction (Active Record) can actually cause severe pain at the infra level! 7. For platform work, Maude personally verifies everything she gets from an LLM. When doing foundational work, Maude pays close attention to verifying the output of LLMs because she believes that ambitious structures can only be built on stable foundations. It’s an interesting approach to separate “foundational” and “non-foundational” work in order to give more attention to the former, most critical, type. 8. Platform and product engineers should rotate more.

articles.content: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.)
